prompt.context: Our client is a coffin maker in the Eastern European country of Maldovia. He has seen substantial change in his market in recent years and is contemplating the future of his business. Up until now, he has been in the business of building high-quality, hand-crafted coffins largely by hand with a skilled labor force. Recently, however, he has become aware of technology that would allow him to build machine-made coffins with much less labor.
prompt.question: Should he invest in this new technology, and should he even remain in the coffin business in the first place?

clarifying_info.q: What is the population of Maldovia?
What is the population growth rate?
What is the average life expectancy?

clarifying_info.a: Assume a flat age distribution (same number of people at every age)

clarifying_info.q: What are the local burial customs?
clarifying_info.a: 75% of deaths are buried in coffins

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of a coffin?
clarifying_info.a: Coffins are priced at $5,000 for a hand-made coffin
Material accounts for 10% of direct cost, labor accounts for 90%. COGS is $4,800 per coffin. Fixed costs are $700,000 per year. All assets are fully depreciated; ignore taxes.

clarifying_info.q: What is the company's market share?
clarifying_info.a: Maldovian Coffins has a 10% market share and a relative market share of about 1

clarifying_info.q: What are the market trends, regulation, or exogenous factors?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the market is expected to continue as it currently is

clarifying_info.q: How much does it cost to invest in the new technology?
What are the cost savings from the new technology?
clarifying_info.a: Material costs remain the same, but labor costs are reduced by 50%

clarifying_info.q: Is the new technology proprietary or exclusive?
clarifying_info.a: The technology is offered by a machine tool company that holds the patent but will not offer exclusivity — they will sell to any competitor
It is not known whether competitors have acquired or are planning to acquire the technology

clarifying_info.q: Will customers notice a difference between hand-made and machine-made coffins?
clarifying_info.a: The quality perceived by the customer is the same or better; the customer will be indifferent between hand-made and machine-made coffins

clarifying_info.q: What are the fixed assets of the business?
clarifying_info.a: Since the firm builds coffins by hand, fixed assets are essentially only the land and improvements, owned outright

clarifying_info.q: What is the book value of the land and improvements?
clarifying_info.a: Book value of land: $20,000; book value of improvements: $80,000; years owned: 48; average real estate appreciation: 6% per year

exhibits.title: Business Valuation Math (Current Operations)
exhibits.shows: A structured calculation layout showing contribution margin, total contribution, and profit computation for the current business
exhibits.data: Contribution Margin = $200/coffin; x 40,000 coffins; x 10% market share; = $800,000; Profit = CM - Fixed Costs = $800,000 - $700,000 = $100,000

exhibits.title: New Technology Cost and Margin Analysis
exhibits.shows: A structured calculation layout showing the revised cost structure, new price, and contribution margin under the new machine-made coffin technology scenario
exhibits.data: Gross Margin = 4%; Labor Cost = $2,160; Material Cost = $480; COGS = $2,640; Price = $2,718; Contribution Margin = $78/coffin

framework: Identify all strategic alternatives (sell business, liquidate assets, continue as-is, invest in new technology)
Value the business under current operations (market size × market share × contribution margin → perpetuity value)
Value the business under liquidation (appreciate book value of assets using rule of 72)
Assess value if new technology is adopted (recalculate costs, project competitive response on pricing, revalue)
Compare all options and recommend the path that maximizes owner value

questions.prompt: What strategic alternatives should the owner consider?
questions.guidance: Candidate should enumerate four options: (1) sell the business to a third party, (2) sell assets and shut down, (3) keep operating as-is, (4) keep operating and invest in new technology. Interviewer should help if not all four are identified, as this framework is the foundation for all subsequent modules.

questions.prompt: How large is the coffin market in Maldovia (number of coffins purchased per year)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm at least 4 ways to estimate market size (e.g., from population + life expectancy, death records, obituary samples, birth rates). Then calculate: with a flat age distribution and 0% growth, 1/75th of 4M people die each year = ~53,333 deaths. 75% are buried in coffins = ~40,000 coffins per year.

math.setup: Population 4M, flat age distribution, avg life expectancy 75 years, 75% buried in coffins

questions.prompt: What is the current value of the business (as a going concern)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate contribution margin, multiply by annual volume and market share to get total contribution, subtract fixed costs to get annual profit, then apply a perpetuity formula. Discount rate of 10% is reasonable.

math.setup: Price $5,000; COGS $4,800; CM = $200/coffin; market = 40,000 coffins; market share = 10%; fixed costs = $700,000; discount rate = 10%

questions.prompt: What is the liquidation value of the business (selling the assets)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm at least 3 ways to value real estate (comparable sales, discounted rental income, appreciation from book value). Then apply rule of 72: at 6% appreciation, value doubles every 12 years. Over 48 years (4 doublings), the $100,000 in assets grows to $1.6M. Since $1.6M > $1M going-concern value, liquidation is more attractive.

math.setup: Book value of land $20,000 + improvements $80,000 = $100,000 total; held 48 years; appreciation 6%/year

questions.prompt: What would be the value of the business if the owner invests in the new technology?
questions.guidance: Key insight: the technology is non-proprietary, so competitors will likely adopt it too, driving down industry costs and ultimately prices. If gross margins remain constant at 4%, new price would be ~$2,718 and the business becomes unprofitable. Candidates may argue for higher margin retention but must acknowledge the competitive threat. Strong candidates note this makes investment unattractive.

math.setup: Current gross margin = $200/$5,000 = 4%; new labor cost = ($4,800 × 90%) × 50% = $2,160; material unchanged = $4,800 × 10% = $480; new COGS = $2,640; assume gross margin maintained at 4%
math.answer: Business becomes unprofitable at -$388,000/year under competitive pricing scenario

brainstorming.prompt: How would you determine the value of the real estate / land and improvements?

categories.name: Comparable Market Transactions
ideas: Look for comparable commercial real estate in the area and determine recent selling prices
Adjust for differences in size, location, and condition

categories.name: Income Approach
ideas: Find comparable commercial real estate and determine rent per square foot
Discount the cash flows generated by renting the property at an appropriate cap rate

categories.name: Cost/Appreciation Approach
ideas: Determine the average rate of appreciation for property in the area
Apply appreciation to the book value of current land and improvements using rule of 72 or compounding

recommendation: The owner should sell the business as soon as possible, targeting approximately $1.6M for the real estate assets, which exceeds the $1M going-concern value
The introduction of non-proprietary machine-making technology creates a credible threat of industry-wide price deflation that would make the business unprofitable; this further supports exiting now
risks: If competitors do not adopt the new technology, the competitive pricing pressure may not materialize and the going-concern value would hold
The real estate valuation is based on historical appreciation; actual market conditions may differ
The owner may not be able to find a buyer quickly at the target price
next_steps: Engage a commercial real estate broker to list the property and obtain independent appraisals
Explore whether a third-party buyer would pay a premium for the business as a going concern (above $1M)
If unable to sell immediately, operate as a cash cow without further investment while continuing to pursue a sale
Do not invest $1M in the new technology given the non-proprietary nature and competitive risk
